The hydrogen stream goes through final purification in which any remaining amounts of carbon oxides are removed from the gas to avoid poisoning the ammonia catalyst. One option for purification is methanation in which CO and CO are 2 converted back to methane to less than 5 ppm (Bartels, 2008). Other options include nitrogen wash or pressure swing adsorption (PSA), in which a highly pure H stream is generated 2 (Pattabathula & Richardson, 2016). The source of N is the process enters via air input to a 2 11 COMPARISON OF COMMERCIAL, STATE-OF-THE-ART, FOSSIL-BASED AMMONIA PRODUCTION secondary reformer which increases methane conversion and heat recovery or via high purity N separated using an air separation unit (Pattabathula & Richardson, 2016). 2 There are other production routes for ammonia via alternative or renewable feedstocks, novel technologies for H and N production, or different chemistries other than the Haber-Bosch 2 2 process. Plastics have been converted to ammonia via gasification at the Showa Denko facility in Japan, which uses a fluidized bed gasifier and has recycled over 1 MM tonnes of plastic during its operation (Resonac, 2024). Renewable energy-driven ammonia production is gaining traction. This approach leverages solar, wind, or hydropower to power electrolyzers for hydrogen production and air separation units for nitrogen generation. The resulting H and N 2 2 are then fed into a conventional Haber-Bosch process . Advanced technologies include solid oxide electrolysis systems that produce ammonia synthesis feed gas (i.e., H and N ) without the 2 2 use of an ASU, which may achieve a 10 percent reduction in energy consumption compared to conventional ammonia production plants (Kakish, 2020). Other advanced technologies include electrocatalytic ammonia production using a novel catalyst that converts air and water directly into NH (Kakish, 2020). 3 1.4 END USES Ammonia is used globally in fertilizers, refrigerants, explosives, plastics, synthetic fibers/resins, and precursors to other chemical compounds (National Minerals Information Center, 2019). In 2019, about 88 percent of ammonia consumed in the United States was used as fertilizer (National Minerals Information Center, 2019). Ammonia is poised to play a crucial role in future energy systems, particularly as a hydrogen carrier and energy storage medium. Projected uses for ammonia include energy storage, electricity generation, and transportation or shipping fuel, and these can be accomplished via direct combustion in engines and turbines, via co-firing in coal boilers, or via conversion in fuel cells. Furthermore, ammonia can be used as a heat transfer agent to aid in phase change and absorption for bulk thermal storage. The benefits of using ammonia as an energy carrier include the existing infrastructure for ammonia production, transport, and storage; its favorable physical properties in terms of energy density and safety; and its lower cost compared to other energy storage alternatives (EERE, 2021) (Golar LNG, 2021) (The Royal Society, 2020) (Crolius, 2021).
